focal_region.annotated_sentence_text:
[Turn 1 USER]
e001	Our small academic software group has built an open tool for exploring archival text collections.
e002	It is not used for medical or individual decisions; it helps researchers find patterns and passages to inspect.
e003	Two labs have used private builds and want us to release a public beta.
e004	The analysis engine is stable on our test collections, but installation is awkward and the documentation assumes people understand our data format.
e005	Half the team wants feedback now.
e006	The maintainers worry a messy release will define our reputation.
[Turn 1 ASSISTANT]
e007	The decision depends on what you want the beta to learn and which failures would be informative rather than merely predictable.
e008	If most early users will fail at installation or formatting, the feedback may tell you what you already know and consume goodwill.
e009	If the private labs have only used familiar collections, a broader beta could reveal important assumptions.
e010	You might delay “public” while expanding a structured preview to users with different data.
[Turn 2 USER]
e011	That is close to what the maintainers say, but the structured preview has been “one more cohort” for six months.
e012	Each time we add users, we find another thing to document before going public.
e013	Meanwhile two volunteer contributors have stopped attending meetings because there is no visible release.
e014	I do not think contributor momentum is superficial.
e015	A tool that is always almost ready can become a private service for our friends.
[Turn 2 ASSISTANT]
e016	Agreed—indefinite preview is itself a product choice, and it can narrow both the community and the evidence you receive.
e017	A public beta can create a focal point for contributors if its limits are explicit.
e018	The maintainers' concern still matters because public access changes the volume and variety of support.
e019	The question may be less “is it ready?” than “what support promise accompanies the release, and can the team sustain that promise?”
[Turn 3 USER]
e020	I am not sure disclaimers solve it.
e021	Researchers often ignore “beta” once they have invested in a workflow.
e022	If we change the data model later, they may feel we broke something even if we warned them.
e023	Also, the two labs want to cite the tool in papers this year.
e024	A public version would make that easier and may help our grant renewal, but I do not want citation pressure to freeze an interface we chose for convenience.
[Turn 3 ASSISTANT]
e025	Then the most consequential commitment may be the data and output format, not the release label.
e026	You could mark some interfaces as experimental while stabilizing a minimal exchange format for saved projects.
e027	But that creates engineering work and may imply more compatibility than you can guarantee.
e028	The publication and grant benefits are real organizational incentives; they should be named openly rather than translated into an argument that users necessarily need the current interface now.
[Turn 4 USER]
e029	You are assuming we can identify a minimal stable format.
e030	Priya, who designed the data layer, says that doing so before seeing stranger collections would formalize the wrong abstractions.
e031	She wants public examples precisely to learn what should be stable.
e032	Our senior maintainer says that is using users to discover architecture at their expense.
e033	They respect each other, but the conversation has become “learning” versus “responsibility,” and both words are doing too much work.
[Turn 4 ASSISTANT]
e034	Those positions may differ on who bears the cost of uncertainty.
e035	Priya expects real use to reveal the right abstractions; the maintainer expects early users to absorb migration and support costs.
e036	A release design could make that cost visible and bounded—for example, limiting the beta to disposable projects or providing an export path—yet either choice may reduce the natural use you wanted to observe.
e037	There may not be a way to learn from committed use without creating some obligation to those users.
[Turn 5 USER]
e038	We learned today that installation is easier than we thought for people using the common package manager, but one private lab had a staff engineer quietly solving problems for everyone.
e039	Their researchers reported a smooth experience because they never saw the setup work.
e040	That makes our private evidence look weaker.
e041	On the other hand, a volunteer wrote a new installer over the weekend and wants real users before polishing it.
e042	I cannot tell whether this argues for release or for another round of testing.
[Turn 5 ASSISTANT]
e043	It argues against treating the private labs as representative, but it does not choose the next step by itself.
e044	The new installer could change the support burden, and public use could test it under real conditions.
e045	A bounded installation test with people who lack staff engineering might answer that question faster than either a full beta or more internal polishing.
e046	Still, if every uncertainty becomes a separate pre-release study, you recreate the endless preview problem you already identified.
[Turn 6 USER]
e047	The team could support a public beta for eight weeks if we rotate office hours, but the senior maintainer will be on leave during the last three weeks.
e048	Priya says that is fine because it forces knowledge sharing.
e049	He says it turns his absence into an experiment other people did not choose.
e050	We can move the date, but then we miss a workshop where many potential users will be together.
e051	The workshop is a real learning opportunity, not only publicity.
[Turn 6 ASSISTANT]
e052	Launching into a known reduction in experienced support is a real risk, and calling it knowledge sharing does not assign the work.
e053	The workshop also offers unusually concentrated feedback.
e054	One compromise is to use the workshop as an announced hands-on preview and schedule the public beta after the maintainer returns.
e055	That preserves some learning while delaying open access, though contributors may reasonably see it as another preview and workshop participants may still form expectations.
[Turn 7 USER]
e056	I am leaning toward releasing an openly downloadable “workshop preview” with a fixed end date, office hours, and no compatibility promise, then deciding on the public beta after we review installation failures and the maintainer returns.
e057	I dislike inventing another label, and I know people can keep downloaded software after the date.
e058	But I also do not want to call it a public beta when our support capacity changes halfway through.
e059	I have not resolved whether citations should be allowed to reference the preview.
[Turn 7 ASSISTANT]
e060	The proposal makes the support window and decision point concrete, but your discomfort is justified: a new label cannot fully control how released software is used.
e061	Citation is the unresolved commitment because it can turn a temporary preview into a durable scholarly object.
e062	You could provide a citable project description without presenting the preview interface as stable, but researchers may still cite the software version they used.
e063	The plan can bound your promise; it cannot make public use temporary in every practical sense.

packet.question: How did the working position or decision change, and does any unresolved qualification remain capable of changing it?
